title: Venial of its kind: disordered object that still does not fight charity
source_text: VII. Peccata venialia ex genere suo vocant, ea quae habent quidem pro objecto rem malam & inordinatam; sed quae charitati Dei & proximi non repugnat. Quale est verbum otiosum, risus nimius, & alia id genus. Et his opponunt peccata mortalia ex genere suo, ut perjurium, adulterium, & similia; quae aperte cum charitate Dei & proximi pugnant.
pass_a_gloss: They call sins venial from their own kind those which indeed have for their object a thing evil and disordered, but which does not fight against the charity of God and neighbor. Such is an idle word, excessive laughter, and other things of that kind. And to these they oppose mortal sins from their own kind, as perjury, adultery, and the like, which openly fight with the charity of God and neighbor.
pass_b_english: A venial-of-its-kind act aims at something disordered that still does not war with charity—idle talk, excess mirth, and the like.
Mortals of their kind (perjury, adultery) openly clash with love of God and neighbor.

choices.why: Classic minor matter in Roman catalogues.
